findings.title: Second downsize definition overrides the existing five-argument version
findings.body: Ruby does not support method overloading. Defining self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) at line 149 replaces self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) at line 145, making the latter dead code. Any existing caller passing separate width and height will now raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, 5 for 4) instead of resizing. The old signature must be preserved or all its callers migrated, e.g. by handling both a String dimension and width/height in one method.

findings.title: Animated GIFs cannot be downsized with a percentage dimension
findings.body: The controller passes "80%" to OptimizedImage.downsize with allow_animation taken from SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When animation is allowed, OptimizedImage.optimize routes GIFs to downsize_instructions_animated/resize_instructions_animated, which passes the dimension to `gifsicle --resize-fit`; gifsicle expects a WIDTHxHEIGHT geometry, not "80%", so it fails and the GIF is never reduced. When animation is not allowed, the non-animated path uses `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame and silently flattens an animated upload into a static image. Either way animated GIF uploads are broken by this feature.

findings.title: Downsize result is ignored while converting a file onto itself
findings.body: OptimizedImage.downsize is invoked with tempfile.path as both input and output and its boolean return value is discarded. convert_with returns false on a failed ImageMagick/gifsicle/ImageOptim run, and an in-place convert that fails or is interrupted can leave the target truncated or partially written. The loop then retries up to five times on that possibly-corrupt file and create_upload proceeds to Upload.create_for with it, so a transient conversion failure turns a valid upload into a corrupt stored file instead of keeping the original or reporting an error.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10 MB client limit ignores site settings and upload type
findings.body: validateUploadedFile previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments each respected the admin-configured limit. Replacing it with a fixed 10 * 1024 makes the client accept files above a site's configured max_image_size_kb/max_attachment_size_kb (attachments are not downsized server-side at all, and images still exceeding the limit after five reductions are rejected by the server with a confusing error after upload), and rejects nothing for sites that configured a limit above 10 MB. The same hardcoding in the 413 handler at line 246 also reports a wrong max_size_kb in the error message for such sites.

findings.title: Synchronous downsizing loop enables expensive processing of huge/decompression-bomb images
findings.body: The change raises the accepted image size to 10 MB (line 55 for URL downloads and the JS limit) and then runs up to five full ImageMagick convert plus ImageOptim passes over the file inside the request/deferred upload job, gated only on compressed file size. A small compressed file can decode to enormous pixel dimensions, so each pass can consume very large CPU/memory, and an attacker can repeat this per upload. There is no pixel-dimension bound or timeout before invoking convert, creating an image-bomb denial-of-service vector that did not exist with the previous size gate.
